title: Errors and Exceptions
oneLiner: What an exception is, reading a stack trace in each language, try/catch/finally versus try/except/else/finally, throw and raise, when to check instead, and the matching exception names.
keyTakeaway: An exception unwinds the call stack until a matching catch or except handles it; finally always runs. Catch specific types, put them before broad ones, and never swallow an exception silently. A C# stack trace lists the failing call first; a Python traceback lists it last, so read Python's from the bottom up.
explanation:
Programs fail: a file is missing, a sensor sends text where a number belongs, a list is empty when the code expected at least one item. When a function hits a problem it can't deal with, it throws (C#) or raises (Python) an exception, an object describing what went wrong. The function stops at that point and the exception travels back up through the functions that called it, a process called unwinding the stack, until some code catches it.

If nothing catches it, the program stops and prints a stack trace: the exception's type and message plus the chain of calls that led there, with file names and line numbers. Learning to read one quickly is one of the most valuable debugging skills there is, so this lesson shows real traces from both languages.

To handle an exception you wrap the risky code in a try block and add a catch (C#) or except (Python) clause for each kind of exception you can actually deal with, plus an optional finally block for cleanup that must happen either way. Your own functions can throw exceptions too, to refuse bad input loudly instead of carrying on with nonsense.

The languages have different habits. C# reserves exceptions for unexpected problems and offers TryParse-style methods for failures you expect. Python code commonly just tries an operation and handles the exception. Both agree that an empty catch block that hides an error is never the answer.
